records.name: Canada
records.current_summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveler warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets.
records.current_localsOnly: Provincial self-declaration LGR, the federal X marker, and the Alberta/Saskatchewan school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks are resident-facing; the 2022 survey data describes residents.
records.current_outOfScope: Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026): police-reported hate crime totalled 4,882 incidents in 2024 (+1% after a 34% jump in 2022-23); incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889 — three consecutive years of increases ended.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 307 redirect loop); the underlying Egale Canada report analyses 2024 hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying page presents quick stats from the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings.

Egale Canada UPR submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in Canada - sexual orientation in the Charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles.

CBC News (Apr 2016): Prince Edward Island amended its Vital Statistics Act so a trans person changes the gender on official documents by declaring their identified gender plus a doctor's letter — the prior surgery requirement removed. A practical document-update pathway in one province.

The Globe and Mail (Jun 2017): the Senate passed Bill C-16 by 67-11, prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression and adding gender identity/expression to the Criminal Code hate-motivation provisions — framed as Canadian leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash.

Ontario Human Rights Commission policy (Part I): lays out the legal context, case law and legislation for sexual-orientation discrimination complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression — official Ontario guidance a visitor/resident can invoke for discrimination recourse.

freshness_all.fact: 2012 UPR shadow-report cited has been overtaken: gender identity/expression added to Criminal Code & CHRA (2017), conversion therapy a crime (2021/22), marriage since 2005. Re-check any 'gap' claims it contained.

records.name: Australia
records.current_summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court's landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability.
records.current_localsOnly: State-level LGR remains a patchwork (not all jurisdictions are self-ID) and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: State LGR patchwork and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying Queensland Human Rights Commission item concerned strengthened discrimination protections for gender-diverse people under Queensland's anti-discrimination law reform.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 400); this was a NSW Parliament bill document (PDF), not retrievable at fetch time.

ANROWS research briefing: maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia — organised exclusionary campaigns, facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures: the live opposition landscape a trans visitor moves through despite strong statutes.

Queensland Parliamentary Library research brief (2003) 'Protecting Transgender Rights under Queensland's Discrimination Law Amendment Act 2002': introduced 'gender identity' as a protected attribute; documents trans people's difficulties with sex designations on passports, licences and birth certificates, high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places.

Organisation Intersex International Australia briefing: argues intersex is not a gender identity and warns against folding intersex into SOGI legal frameworks (recommends SOGIESC terminology) — relevant to how Australian gender-diversity protections are scoped.

Australian Lesbian & Gay Archives, 'Towards Homosexual Equality in Australian Criminal Law - A Brief History' (Carbery, 2nd ed. 2014): state-by-state history of decriminalisation, from British-inherited buggery laws (death penalty in Victoria until 1949) through reform - historical legal context for Australia's current framework.

freshness_all.fact: Marriage equality (2017); federal hate-crime offence Feb 2025; conversion-therapy bans ~85% of pop. since Oct 2024 — far beyond pre-2017 state.

records.name: New Zealand
records.current_summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit; the Counting Ourselves survey found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats). New Zealand's global-progressive reputation outruns its current street climate.

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.
records.current_localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR regime (2023) and the Law Commission review are resident-facing; the Counting Ourselves survey data describes residents.
records.current_outOfScope: Counting Ourselves data is resident-survey-based; healthcare gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: RNZ (17 Apr 2024), Official Information Act data: 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023 vs 161 in 2022 — a 42% rise — with police saying the figure likely understates true anti-trans hate, and a spike in the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited (March 2023). For this record: the quantified police dataset with the undercount caveat.

RNZ (27 Feb 2025), Counting Ourselves survey: almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the past four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence — the first clear population picture of violence against these communities. For this record: survey-based prevalence figures.

New Zealand Law Commission Issues Paper 53 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024): a review of the protections in the Human Rights Act 1993 for transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics - official law-reform consultation document.

The Spinoff opinion (2 Jul 2024) by Jennifer Shields: after a spate of rainbow event cancellations and a 2023 Posie Parker protest, calls for more security for rainbow communities — noting statutory wins (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 easing ID correction; Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022) alongside a worsening street climate. For this record: community-safety assessment dated mid-2024 with the recent statutory wins named.

Spartacus Gay Travel Index 2026 (Feb 2026): annual index measuring the legal situation and living conditions for queer people in each country across 18 categories (marriage to death penalty); color-coded from dark green (most liberal) to red (most dangerous); explains its rating system including negative points for death-penalty laws and Sharia application.

glbtq encyclopedia entry on New Zealand (Andrew Matzner, 2004): long history of liberal reform (women's suffrage 1893); Gay Liberation Front emerged April 1972; decriminalisation followed years of activism; Georgina Beyer reportedly the first transsexual in the world to achieve national office; 13th country with equal marriage (2013).

PrideNZ.com: archive of over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa NZ's LGBTQIA+ communities, a rainbow timeline, over 18,000 GayNZ.com articles (2001-2017), and Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates. For this record: a usable local community/archive resource base (context, not risk).

records.name: North Macedonia
records.current_summary:
North Macedonia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and Skopje hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and there is no legal gender recognition.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard Balkan street-hostility caution.
records.current_localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the justice-system non-response affects resident victims.
records.current_outOfScope: Justice-system non-response and LGR absence are resident-facing/climate.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia: hate speech remained serious with countless reports and no meaningful state response (European Commission country report concurs); in September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with SOGI aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code; ECRI called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Global Voices (30 March 2024): TransFormA’s March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility — "we march bravely" — while noting a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

ILGA-Europe/ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia chapter with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia: top priority is Legal Gender Recognition — the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review.
US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for North Macedonia: official assessment including the SOGI section - anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.

Washington Blade (13 October 2023): economic analysis with Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI groups quantifying how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of Serbia and North Macedonia — discrimination cast as a measurable drag on growth and jobs, without country-specific figures in the piece.

Balkan Insight (February 2012): ILGA-Europe’s Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at −2 on the 17-to−7 scale — the only Balkan country in the "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination.

Balkan Insight (July 2014): the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman — ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption — as an early act of the re-elected Gruevski government, needing two-thirds of MPs with the conservative DPA expected to supply the extra votes.

records.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
records.current_summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress. Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report: negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in Republika Srpska and rural areas.
records.current_localsOnly: No legal gender recognition framework and restricted healthcare access — resident-facing; the precarious position documented in the Pink Report describes residents' situation.
records.current_outOfScope: Entity-level (Republika Srpska) hostility varies; LGR absence is resident-facing.

sources.claim: Sarajevo Open Centre, Pink Report 2024 (13 Jun 2024): annual report on LGBTI human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina — the past year saw a number of negative events with significant impact, and the long-visible worsening trend is 'becoming increasingly evident'. For this record: current national climate assessment from the leading local monitor.

Balkan Diskurs (25 Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice — the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on 'completed' medical transition, constraints described as discriminatory and degrading. For this record: the documentation pathway a trans person navigating the system faces — resident-facing, not a border issue.

Human Rights Watch (4 Feb 2014): violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers — Sarajevo Open Centre staff said they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier; HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of attackers. For this record: precedent that organised anti-LGBT violence occurs even WITH prior police coordination (dated 2014, context for later attacks).

GlobalGayz (2012): same-sex conduct decriminalised in the Federation of BiH (1996) and Republika Srpska (1998) via the two entities' own criminal codes; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation but omitted gender identity as originally intended. For this record: entity-level legal baseline plus the pre-2016 gender-identity protection gap.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): BiH's amended Anti-Discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity with correct local terminology — SOC co-presented the amendments with the Agency for Gender Equality after fall-2015 public consultations. For this record: the statutory protection now on the books at state level.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation explicitly naming sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances — SOC coordinator Vladana Vasić confirming the long-sought coalition win. For this record: entity-level sentencing enhancement for bias attacks in FBiH (RS runs its own separate regime).

freshness_all.fact: Legal state-wide (1996/98/2003); entities restrict marriage to opposite-sex couples; uneven protections, 2023 activist attack; ILGA-2024 picture stands.

records.name: Georgia
records.current_summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament passed the Russia-style law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region's harshest legislative package outside Russia itself. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi apartment; mourners and AP drew a direct line between the law's rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases, still unimplemented). Georgia's visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2024 law's LGR ban and transition-healthcare ban are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors.
records.current_outOfScope: The 2024 law’s healthcare and LGR provisions are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors.

sources.claim: BBC (Sep 2024): trans model and influencer Kesaria Abramidze was killed just one day after the Georgian parliament passed the anti-LGBTI law; German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Georgia's anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation' — after the stabbing death of trans actress-model Kesaria Abramidze, Russia-style 'gay propaganda' laws stoke fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Georgia: the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

WISG et al. report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers (5 Aug 2024) on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions in Georgia: recommends urgent action — effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

IWPR Global Voices (May 2012): 'Georgian Laws Discriminate on Transgender Rights' - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity doesn't match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers in Georgia.

OC Media (Jun 2019): Georgia's Interior Ministry declared Tbilisi Pride 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks' (programme 18–23 June); organisers reported a week of pressure from an 'unidentified government official' to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it — the country's first-ever pride.

records.name: Armenia
records.current_summary:
Armenia demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the Georgian or Russian type — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia's 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific protection statute. Yerevan has a small organised community (Pink Armenia, Right Side — a trans-led NGO), but visibility carries real risk.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central Yerevan; police response unreliable.
records.current_localsOnly: The medicalised legal gender recognition practice and the absence of a SOGI protection statute are resident-facing; a visitor's documents come from their home country.
records.current_outOfScope: Protection-statute absence and LGR medicalisation are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Pink Human Rights Defender NGO annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024. Documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech - including a chapter on pressure around a transgender individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Equaldex comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia: Armenia decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections 'ambiguous' since 2022; no SOGI discrimination protections; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low (5/100).

ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Unzipped: Gay Armenia blog (May 2012): neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan - Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via CCTV - documents anti-LGBT hate violence in Armenia.

The Guardian (April 2019): Armenia's first registered trans woman, Lilit Martirosyan, received death threats (including MPs calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination - documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

records.name: Azerbaijan
records.current_summary:
Azerbaijan is dangerous for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in Baku in July 2023; a second trans woman's murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech. Trans people face total economic marginalisation (black-market work, precarious housing).

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world's more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling found violations in Azerbaijan's treatment of LGBTI applicants.

For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented.
records.current_localsOnly: The economic marginalisation data (black-market work, precarious housing) is resident-facing; the police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant.
records.current_outOfScope: Economic exclusion data is resident-facing; police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents the March murder of a trans woman in Baku met with an inadequate police investigation; state-affiliated Real TV airing discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding trans healthcare access; a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out; and an April ECtHR ruling on the September 2017 police arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, which Azerbaijan acknowledged in 2019.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents a July police raid on a private birthday party where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing; QueeRadar monitoring found 77% of 428 analysed media pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people; and an activist being told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

OC Media feature by Ali Malikov on trans people in Azerbaijan: discrimination has direct economic impacts - trans people are rejected from jobs and housing, pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. Profiles 'Durdana', 29, arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

HRW (Oct 2017): Azerbaijan's anti-gay crackdown — police raids in Baku (Sept 2017) detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented; HRW called for investigation and release.

Gender & Development Social Union shadow report to CEDAW (44th session) on discrimination and violence against lesbian, bisexual and transgender people in Azerbaijan: documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia/transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves 200+ LBT people.

The Guardian (Sept 2017): outcry as Azerbaijan police launch crackdown on the LGBT community - at least 60 people imprisoned or fined after raids in the capital; part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

freshness_all.fact: No protections, hostile enforcement: mass Baku arrest waves with beatings/forced exams; strong stigma; the ILGA-2025 review picture remains current.
